contentSummary: Family Members• Father; A man who is the parent of a child. He cares for, guides, and supports the child.• Mother; A woman who is the parent of a child. She gives birth to or raises the child.• Brother; A boy or man who shares the same parents with you.• Sister; A girl or woman who shares the same parents with you.• Uncle; The brother of your father or mother. In some Af2rican cultures, your father’s brother or your mother’s brother is also seen as your father.• Aunt; The sister of your father or mother. In some African cultures, your mother’s sister or your father’s sister is also seen as your mother.• Cousin; The child of your aunt or uncle.Types of Families• Nuclear Family; Parents (father and mother) and their children living together.• Extended Family; A big family that includes parents, children, grandparents, uncles, aunts, cousins, and in-laws.• Single Parent Family; One parent raising children alone. This can happen because of death, divorce, separation, or parents living apart.• Child-Headed Family; A family where children take care of their brothers and sisters because parents are not present.• Guardian-Headed Family; A family where someone who is not the parent (like grandparents, uncles, aunts, or family friends) takes care of the children. contentSummary: Human rights are basic rights that every person has from birth. These rights help people live with dignity, safety, and respect. Human rights apply to all people, including children, regardless of where they live or who they are. In this sub topic you will guide learners to recognize their rights that promotes peace, respect, equality, and good relationships among people in the family, school, and community. Children have special rights because they need care, love, and protection to grow well. When people respect human rights, everyone can live in peace, be treated equally, and have good relationships at home, school, and in the community. However, should exercise these rights responsibly.Some examples of basic human rights include• Right to Life; every child has the right to live and be safe from harm.• Right to Food; every child should have enough healthy food to grow strong and not be hungry.• Right to Shelter; every child should have a safe home to live in, away from rain, cold, and danger.• Right to Health Care; every child should get help from a doctor or nurse when sick or hurt.• Right to Education; every child should go to school to learn and prepare for the future.• Right to Protection; every child should be kept safe from abuse, neglect, and violence.• Keep people safe; human rights protect everyone from harm, abuse, and unfair treatment.• Protect children; they stop children from being hurt, forced to work, or treated badly.• Bring peace; when people respect each other’s rights, there is less fighting and more understanding.• Teach fairness; human rights help people treat each other equally, no matter their differences.• Help children grow; rights like food, shelter, health care, and education help children grow strong, learn, and feel loved.• Prepare for the future; respecting rights helps children become responsible and helpful members of society.• Help children , practise their rights responsibly
learnerActivities: Reporting human rights abuses to relevant authorities (Parents, responsible adults, teachers)

contentSummary: Obligations and duties are responsibilities that citizens must carry out to keep peace, order, and fairness in society. When citizens obey laws, respect others, and care for their community, the nation becomes safe and united. These actions also support growth and development for everyone. In this sub-topic you will help learners demonstrate patriotism for their country. Abuse is never the child’s fault.Forms of Abuse:1. Physical Abuse (Hurting the body)o When someone hits, kicks, shakes, or burns a child.o No one has the right to hurt a child’s body.2. Emotional Abuse (Hurting the feelings)o When someone uses mean words like shouting, calling names, or making a child feel scared.o These words hurt the heart even if they don’t leave marks.3. Neglect (Not caring properly)o When adults don’t give a child food, clean water, clothes, or a safe place to sleep.o Also when they don’t take a sick child to the clinic.4. Child Labour (Dangerous work)o Helping with small chores at home is okay.o But forcing a child to do heavy or dangerous work, or stopping them from going to school, is child labour.Every child has the right to be safe and protected from harm. If you or someone you know is being hurt, it is important to speak up. Children should stay away from unsafe situations and report any form of abuse to trusted adults such as parents or guardians, teachers, community leaders, or police officers.'Assessment'Ruth notices that her neighbour, a young child named Kelvin, is often left alone at home. Sub-Topic 4.6.1. Elements of Weather and Climate.
contentSummary: In our daily lives, we need to move from place to place and share information with others. The way we do this depends on where we live, what resources we have, and the type of message we want to send. In Zambia, people use both traditional and modern forms of transport and communication. In this subtopic, you will help your learners to explore different forms of transport and communication services available in your community and around the country.Specific Competence 4.5.1.1. Recognize different forms of Transport and Communication Services Social Studies Teaching Module Learning ActivitiesActivity Exploring different forms of Transport and Communication Services Transport (walking, scotch carts, cycling, riding, motor vehicles...) Communication: (messenger, drum, letter, telex, land phone, cellphone, internet) Learning EnvironmentThe Digital communication tools are apps or websites we use to talk to others, share news, and learn new things. Here are some examples:• Email (e.g., Gmail); used to send formal messages, homework, and letters to teachers or family.• WhatsApp; a messaging app to chat with friends and family, share pictures, and make voice or video calls.• Facebook; a social media site where people can share updates, photos, and videos with their friends.• TikTok; an app for creating and watching short, entertaining videos. Social Studies • YouTube; a video-sharing platform where you can watch educational videos, music, and tutorials.• X (formerly Twitter); a platform for sharing short messages (tweets) and news.Rules for Responsible Use of Digital Communication Tools1. Be kind; always use kind words. Never use digital tools to bully or be mean to others.2. Protect your privacy; never share your full name, home address, phone number, school name, or passwords with people you only know online.3. Ask for permission; always ask a parent or teacher before downloading a new app or posting a photo or video.4. Think before you click; before you send a message or post something, ask yourself: "Is it true? Is it helpful? Is it kind?"5. Keep personal information safe; your family's private information is also private. Don't share it online.6. Tell a trusted adult; if you see something that makes you feel scared, sad, or uncomfortable, or if someone is being mean, tell a parent, teacher, or trusted adult immediately.7. Balance your time; remember to spend time playing outside, reading, and talking to family in person, not just on a screen. Weather and climate are made up of important elements like temperature, rainfall, wind, humidity, and air pressure. These elements help us describe the atmosphere in a place for a short time (weather) or over many years (climate). In this sub-topic learners will use appropriate instruments to measure weather and climate for example thermometers, rain gauge, wind vanes, and barometers. & 2 Rainfall• Provides water for plants, animals, and people.• Too much = floods; too little = drought.• Fills rivers, lakes, and dams.• Instrument: Rain Gauge Social Studies Teaching ModuleWind• Moving air.• Gentle wind is comfortable; strong wind can cause damage.• Helps dry clothes, spread seeds, and pollinate plants.• Can produce electricity.• Instruments: Wind Vane (direction), Anemometer (speed)Sunshine• Gives heat and light.• Helps plants grow (photosynthesis).• Too much = very hot; too little = cold.• Helps dry crops and clothes.• Instrument: Sunshine Recorder (or teacher shows pictures)Clouds• Form when water vapor cools and condenses.• Dark clouds - rain; light clouds - fair weather.• Provide shade and show weather changes.• Instrument: Observation (looking at the sky)Humidity• Amount of moisture (water vapor) in the air.• High humidity - sticky and wet (rainy season).• Low humidity - dry (dry season).• Helps rainfall formation and plant growth.• Instrument: Hygrometer
